facts: Coffee beans are seeds from the fruit of a coffee plant.
Coffee fruit is often called a cherry.
Unroasted coffee beans are known as green coffee.
Roasting changes both the colour and chemistry of coffee beans.
Arabica and robusta are the two main types of commercially grown coffee.
Coffee plants belong to the same botanical family as gardenias.
Espresso is brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee.
Instant coffee is brewed coffee that has been dried.
Decaffeinated coffee usually retains a small amount of caffeine.
The origin of the phrase cup of Joe is disputed.
Chocolate comes from seeds inside cacao pods.
Cacao seeds are fermented before being dried and processed into chocolate.
White chocolate contains cocoa butter but not the dark cocoa solids.
Chocolate was consumed as a drink long before modern chocolate bars.
Cocoa butter is the fat naturally present in cacao seeds.
Chocolate can absorb smells from nearby foods.
A pale coating on chocolate can come from fat or sugar crystals, not mould.
Tempering helps chocolate set with a glossy surface and a clean snap.
Chocolate contains caffeine as well as another stimulant called theobromine.
A mocha combines coffee with chocolate.
A chessboard has 64 squares.
Each player begins a standard chess game with sixteen pieces.
A knight can jump over other chess pieces.
A bishop stays on the same square colour throughout the game.
Castling moves a king and a rook in the same turn.
A pawn reaching the far end of the board can become a queen.
Pawn promotion can give a player more than one queen.
Stalemate ends a chess game in a draw, not a win.
Chess clocks track each player's thinking time separately.
Chess developed from earlier games, including India's chaturanga.
Glass is a solid, not a very slow-flowing liquid.
Glass lacks the regularly repeating atomic pattern found in a crystal.
Obsidian is naturally occurring volcanic glass.
Most ordinary bottles and windows use soda-lime glass.
Glass can be drawn into fibres thinner than a human hair.
Optical fibres carry signals using light travelling through glass.
Borosilicate glass tolerates temperature changes better than ordinary window glass.
Annealing means cooling glass in a controlled way to relieve internal stresses.
Laminated glass holds broken fragments together with a layer between glass sheets.
Different ingredients can give glass different colours.
A rainbow is a full circle, although the ground usually hides its lower portion.
Two people standing apart do not see light from exactly the same rainbow droplets.
Rainbows form when light bends and reflects inside water droplets.
A double rainbow's outer arc has its colours in reverse order.
The space between a primary and secondary rainbow often looks darker.
Moonlight can produce a rainbow, known as a moonbow.
A rainbow's colours blend continuously rather than forming exactly seven separate stripes.
The Sun is behind you when you see an ordinary sunlight rainbow.
A fine spray from a garden hose can create a rainbow.
An aeroplane passenger can sometimes see a complete circular rainbow.
Auroras glow when energetic particles excite gases high in the atmosphere.
The northern lights are also called the aurora borealis.
The southern lights are called the aurora australis.
Oxygen can produce green light in an aurora.
Oxygen can also produce red auroral light at higher altitudes.
Nitrogen contributes blue and purplish colours to auroras.
Auroras often appear as moving curtains rather than a uniform glow.
Strong geomagnetic storms can make auroras visible far from the poles.
Earth's magnetic field helps guide particles involved in auroras.
Auroras occur on other planets as well as Earth.
Snow looks white because its many ice surfaces scatter light.
Snow crystals can form needles and columns, not just star shapes.
Temperature and humidity influence a growing snow crystal's shape.
A snowflake's sixfold structure reflects the arrangement of molecules in ice.
Many real snowflakes are irregular rather than perfectly symmetrical.
Snow crystals can grow directly from water vapour.
Colliding snow crystals can stick together to form larger flakes.
Snowflakes often begin growing around tiny airborne particles.
Falling snow crystals can collect supercooled droplets that freeze onto them.
A snow crystal's journey through changing cloud conditions influences its final shape.
Lightning is a giant electrical discharge.
Much lightning stays within clouds rather than striking the ground.
Thunder comes from air expanding rapidly after lightning heats it.
Lightning can strike the same place repeatedly.
Lightning flashes can contain several separate electrical strokes.
Volcanic eruptions can produce lightning in their ash clouds.
Lightning sometimes occurs during snowstorms.
A lightning flash can reach the ground far from the rain beneath its storm.
Lightning can fuse sandy ground into glassy formations called fulgurites.
Lightning can start wildfires.
Molten rock underground is called magma; at the surface it is called lava.
Volcanic ash consists of tiny rock and glass fragments, not burned wood.
Many volcanoes lie beneath the ocean.
Shield volcanoes have broad, gently sloping sides.
Some volcanoes form above hot spots far from plate boundaries.
Volcanic eruptions release gases as well as molten rock.
Pumice can be light enough to float because it contains so many gas bubbles.
A caldera is a large depression often formed when a volcano's summit collapses.
Volcanic mudflows can carry water, ash and rock down valleys.
Not every volcano is a cone-shaped mountain.
